title: Load Shedding
subtitle: Proactively dropping excess low-priority requests at the edge to preserve goodput under overload.
keyTakeaways: Without load shedding, an overloaded server's **Goodput** (useful responses completed before client timeout) drops to zero due to queueing delay.
Shed load as early and cheaply as possible: prioritizing requests by business criticality (`CRITICAL > HIGH > BATCH/CRAWLER`).
LIFO (Last-In, First-Out) queues with CoDel adaptive queue timeouts outperform FIFO queues during overload spikes.

sections.heading: 1. Architectural Fundamentals & Core Mechanics
sections.body: When a service provisioned for 1,000 RPS suddenly receives 2,500 RPS, a naive server queues all 2,500 requests in memory. Soon, the queue grows so deep that every single request sits waiting in the queue for 3 seconds before a worker thread even looks at it. Since the client timeout is 1 second, **100% of clients have already disconnected**, yet the server spends 100% of its CPU processing dead requests! Although raw *throughput* looks high, **goodput** (successful responses delivered within the client's deadline) collapses to zero. **Load Shedding** prevents this cliff by immediately rejecting excess requests (`HTTP 503 Service Unavailable`) in microseconds so the remaining 1,000 RPS complete in 10ms.
bullets: **Core Architectural Principle**: Without load shedding, an overloaded server's **Goodput** (useful responses completed before client timeout) drops to zero due to queueing delay.
**Problem Space & Invariants**: Shed load as early and cheaply as possible: prioritizing requests by business criticality (`CRITICAL > HIGH > BATCH/CRAWLER`).
**System Boundary**: Operates across client network dispatch, gateway queuing, thread execution pools, and persistent storage I/O.

sections.heading: 2. Architectural Patterns & Implementation Topologies
sections.body: Distributed architectures apply specific implementation patterns and topologies for Load Shedding:
bullets: **FIFO Queueing Without Load Shedding**: Provides fair arrival ordering under normal load (< 70% utilization). Best suited for Offline asynchronous job queues with no interactive client deadline.

**Priority-Tiered Adaptive Load Shedding + LIFO**: Guarantees near-100% goodput and sub-50ms latency for surviving high-priority requests even at 5x overload. Best suited for High-scale API gateways, tier-0 microservices, and transactional databases.
**Reject Cheaply**: Shed requests before parsing large JSON bodies, allocating heap objects, or touching databases.
**Adaptive Concurrency Limits (Little's Law $L = \lambda W$)**: Dynamically adjust concurrency limits using TCP Vegas / Gradient algorithms (measuring `minRTT / sampleRTT` queue inflation).

**Rate Limiting vs Load Shedding**: Rate limiting enforces per-tenant fairness quotas regardless of server health; Load Shedding protects local server survival when physical resources (CPU, memory, event loop lag, in-flight concurrency) approach saturation.
**Session Cohort Pinning**: Shed by deterministic `hash(user_id) % 100` rather than random per-request coin flips so accepted users finish their full transaction flow.

sections.heading: 3. Production Strengths: Where & How to Apply
sections.body: Production deployments apply Load Shedding across targeted operational scenarios:
bullets: **Where to Use: High-Impact Scenarios**: Optimal for Offline asynchronous job queues with no interactive client deadline, suited for environments requiring Fair arrival ordering under normal load (< 70% utilization).

**Where to Use: High-Throughput Scenarios**: Recommended for High-scale API gateways, tier-0 microservices, and transactional databases, where Guarantees near-100% goodput and sub-50ms latency for surviving high-priority requests even at 5x overload.
**How to Use: Engineering Implementation**: Not all requests have equal business value. Always establish explicit thresholds, measurement baselines, and automated monitoring.
**Architectural Leverage**: Provides predictable resource boundaries, bounds blast radius, and optimizes cost per transaction.

sections.heading: 4. Failure Modes & Trade-Offs: When to Avoid
sections.body: Improper implementation of Load Shedding introduces operational bottlenecks and failure modes:
bullets: **Where to Avoid: Trade-Off Bottlenecks**: Avoid when constraints cannot tolerate: catastrophic latency inflation under overload; every request in the queue times out (0% goodput).
**Where to Avoid: Complexity Ceiling**: Avoid when operational requirements do not justify: requires propagating request priority headers and calibrating shedding thresholds.
**Catastrophic Failure Modes**: Uncalibrated parameters can trigger queue exhaustion, thread starvation, cascading retry storms, and tail latency amplification.
**Operational Overhead**: Requires continuous observability (p95/p99 latency tracking, saturation alerts, and distributed tracing across hop boundaries).

sections.heading: 5. Staff+ Engineering Verdict & Interview Playbook
sections.body: Technical guidelines and evaluation criteria for Load Shedding:
bullets: **Staff+ Golden Rule**: LIFO (Last-In, First-Out) queues with CoDel adaptive queue timeouts outperform FIFO queues during overload spikes.

**Staff+ Interview Playbook**: Distinguish **Rate Limiting** (customer-centric fairness at the edge) from **Load Shedding** (server-centric survival based on real-time CPU/queue saturation) and mention **Goodput vs Throughput**.
